en: His voice drove life from men.
When he advanced he scattered nations;
His swooping was like an eagle's.
Look upon his gray-maned valor:
It was like the very eye of Kökchö.
Karadöö, a mass of calamity,
Was just like Semetey himself.
His early word had come late:
Against Kyyaz, son of Bagysh,
He now stood ready to meet him,
Start the conflict,
Match him and take revenge.
If his strength sufficed, he would fight;
Karadöö's purpose, his heart's desire,
Was to take his distant vengeance.
He mourned Semetey,
Would make war upon the hero Kyyaz,
Would set Külchoro free,
And fight Kanchoro.
In Semetey's hands
He had been a darling to cradle.
If you ask about Karadöö,
“What will my future be?” he wondered—
This was the omen he chose:
“If my divination proves true,
I shall slaughter Küzhürmön.
If my divination is false,
I shall die at the wrestler's hand.”
So saying, Karadöö
Whipped the gray five-year-old beneath him
To right and left,
Spurred it on both sides,
And turned the champion steed's head.
Facing Küzhürmön,
He thundered forward and lowered his spear.
Before anyone could say a word,
In the blink of an eye:
“The pommel of the Akkangky saddle—
If my spear slips beyond it,
Let it strike the crown of his very heart!”
He charged and struck.
God forbid anyone should behold it:
Dust whirled everywhere,
And the whole arena ran with blood.
To see what would become of Karadöö,
The people cried out and filled the ground.
Such was the deed they saw.
As the two fought with spears,
Their spears shattered noisily;
White splinters from the spear points
Flew buzzing into the sky.
The brutally striking spears
Snapped across the middle.
The stirrup straps
Were sliced to little pieces.
Küzhürmön and Karadöö
Fought a mighty spear contest;
The heroes staked their lives
And crashed against each other.
The people roared in tumult,
The women raised a black lament.
Karadöö and Küzhürmön
Met with spears extended;
Neither hero retreated,
And they smashed together.
Each sought a warrior's stratagem;
When their spears were spent,
They hewed at each other with battle-axes.
The Alangir bow and painted arrow—
Told aloud, it is a dreadful tale.
All their axes shattered,
Leaving only shafts in their hands.
The people cried out in tumult;
The nation shouted in uproar.
The blessing of a holy man had touched him:
The hero Kutu of the Zhediger,
Karadöö's adoptive father,
Galloped the Surbuzul forward,
Turned toward Karadöö,
And handed him a fresh spear:
“The fur collar of my coat,
My foal, hero Karadöö!
Be among those who survive;
Fight the mighty wrestler Küzhürmön
Without rest for seven days!
If you are a hero, be a bullet;
If you are brave, be fierce!
Stand firm and give no ground;
Strive for honor and every stratagem.
Ah, Karadöö, my foal,
A bay colt fit for pursuit
Is not born from an ordinary mare;
When your father grows forlorn,
No son like you, Karadöö, will be born.
Stand face to face,
And strike your pole with all your might!
When the great multitude of Zhediger
Looks upon your spectacle,
May the spear you thrust shatter;
May the champion horse you strike squarely
Fall stretched upon its belly.
When you advance and strike firmly,
May the spear be hung up for measuring.
Let your fame spread openly
Through the people, my foal:
‘Kutu's son is mighty!’
Let old men and all who see him
Despair of their lives,
Saying, ‘Küzhürmön is a wrestler!’
You are alone—be fierce;
Let the multitude despair of life.
Though poor, be generous;
Be sudden enough to scorch stone,
And let the rich despair of life.
If you are a hero, be a wrestler;
Let the khan despair of life.
When you thrust, thrust firmly;
Take aim and spear Küzhürmön.
Let him spend his wrathful strength;
Let Küzhürmön, who entered for the prize,
Cast away all care for life.
Küzhürmön, who boasts of courage—
That champion famous among the people,
Bull-chested and rash-tempered,
That swaggering man swollen with pride—
Spear him squarely and strike true;
Take aim, seize him, and strike firmly!
Let them shout, ‘Küzhürmön has flown from his horse!’
Let the Kyrgyz carry this tale,
The people shouting in excitement;
Let your strength and courage
Please the gathered nation.
Let it become a tale among all the people.
Extend your spear and hold your guard;
Do not flounder, my foal,
Hold your body firmly and do not hurry.
May Küzhürmön's strength depart
And his clothes and armor come apart;
Let Kutu's son be revealed,
And Küzhürmön called a clumsy wrestler!
Hero, add the gray kulan to the herd;
In your father's old age,
Let him be counted among men
By being called the father of a wrestler!”
Kutu came and spoke these words,
A wondrous marvel to those who understood,
And placed the spear in his hand.
Karadöö set out on his course.
When his father Kutu had spoken,
Delivered his words and turned back,
Karadöö inherited those words.
Such was Karadöö's way:
Without looking around,
Before the teeming Zhediger people,
He spared his life for nothing.
Karadöö gathered his strength;
Sparks flew from his great nostrils,
And fire flashed from both eyes.
“Will this wretched soul not see
The decree written upon its brow?
When its days and water are exhausted,
Does a person not die in the end?
Against thundering Küzhürmön
I shall thrust my spear with all my might;
Against the wrestler who boasts of strength,
I shall clash and fight with the spear
And win one prize from him.
If I cannot do that, this wretched soul
Shall face a wrestler like Küzhürmön
And be cast down.
I shall dart like a merlin,
Come out along his flank,
And drive Küzhürmön, the people's wrestler,
Headfirst into a pit.”
So saying, Karadöö
Turned the gray champion steed's head.
“The face of the elbow,
The vulnerable dark ribs,
The middle between them—
That is the place to spear.
Unless Küzhürmön is a mountain,
He cannot withstand the spear;
This is the moment he will tumble.”
With speed beyond reckoning,
He reached him in a flash;
Karadöö struck Küzhürmön
And drove past with a booming blow.
From the place he had struck,
Strips of fine cloth streamed out.
The people cried out in tumult
And rejoiced for Karadöö.
The boastful Küzhürmön,
Like a mountain falling,
Was hurled from his champion steed
And lay stretched along the earth.
He fell sprawling headlong
And drove into the arena floor.
When Küzhürmön came off his horse,
The people cried, “Karadöö has won!”
The crowd roared in uproar,
A tumult that split the sky.
Karadöö, son of the hero Kutu,
Made his wrestling strength known;
The people despaired for their lives,
Saying he was a formidable hero.
“A broad-trousered, wide-chested
Wrestler has come;
He is a wrestler who brings slaughter
Upon anyone who fights him,
A wrestler who brings torment
Upon anyone who faces him.
When his rib bones mature,
When the flesh of his calves fills out,
When the weakness of childhood departs
And he turns fully toward heroism,
When Karadöö becomes such a man,
He will maintain a court and become khan,
Become a man of standing,
A man forged of steel.
He will rule the people and sustain a nation—
Ah... he will become a true man and wrestler!”
He had staked and won the prize.
With your elder Kutman at their head,
They began dividing the countless treasure,
The myriad livestock,
And every one of the many prizes.
When they divided the winnings,
They took red-tailed camels
And, what a wonder, many kinds of livestock.
The most skillful found their share:
They took dark woolly camels;
The finest young champions
Took black-blazed mares.
Their hearts were at ease;
Those who won prizes became rich.
But the hero Karadöö,
Without letting a coin touch his person,
Did not tie even a single mare,
Calling it his booty, to his lead rope.
He took no goods from the spoils.
The sign of his divination came true;
Their hearts were at ease—
Karadöö had won the contest.
